title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Levin pulled on his big boots and, for the first time, a cloth jacket instead of his fur cloak, and went out to look after his farm, stepping over streams of water that flashed in the sunshine and dazzled his eyes, treading one moment on ice and the next into sticky mud.

Spring is the time for plans and projects. And as he came out into the farmyard, Levin, like a tree in spring that does not know what form will be taken by the young shoots and twigs imprisoned in its swelling buds, hardly knew what undertakings he was about to begin in the farm work that was so dear to him. But he felt that he was full of the most splendid plans and projects. First of all he went to the cattle. The cows had been let out into their paddock, and their smooth sides were already shining with their new, sleek spring coats; they basked in the sunshine and lowed to go to the meadow. Levin gazed admiringly at the cows he knew so intimately, down to the slightest detail of their condition, and gave orders for them to be driven out into the meadow, and for the calves to be let into the paddock. The herdsman ran off gaily to get ready for the meadow. The cowherd girls, picking up their petticoats, ran splashing through the mud with bare legs, still white, not yet brown from the sun, waving brushwood in their hands, chasing the calves that frolicked in the joy of spring.

After admiring the young ones of that year, who were particularly fine — the early calves were the size of a peasant's cow, and Pava's daughter, at three months, was as big as a yearling — Levin gave orders for a trough to be brought out and for them to be fed in the paddock. But it turned out that since the paddock had not been used during the winter, the hurdles made in the autumn for it had been broken. He sent for the carpenter, who, according to his orders, was supposed to be at work on the thrashing machine. But it turned out that the carpenter was repairing the harrows, which should have been repaired before Lent. This was very annoying to Levin. It was annoying to encounter that everlasting slovenliness in the farm work he had been fighting with all his might for so many years. The hurdles, as he learned, not being wanted in winter, had been carried to the cart-horses' stable, and there broken, since they were of light construction, only meant for feeding calves. Moreover, it was apparent too that the harrows and all the agricultural implements, which he had directed should be looked over and repaired in the winter — for which very purpose he had hired three carpenters — had not been put into repair, and the harrows were being repaired when they ought to have been harrowing the field. Levin sent for his bailiff, but immediately set off himself to look for him. The bailiff, beaming all over, like everyone that day, in a sheepskin bordered with astrachan, came out of the barn, twisting a bit of straw in his hands.
"Why isn't the carpenter at the thrashing machine?"
"Oh, I meant to tell you yesterday — the harrows need repairing. It's time they got to work in the fields."
"But what were they doing in the winter, then?"
"But what did you want the carpenter for?"
"Where are the hurdles for the calves' paddock?"
"I ordered them to be got ready. What can one do with peasants like these?" said the bailiff, waving a hand.

"It's not those peasants, it's this bailiff!" Levin said, getting angry. "Why, what do I keep you for?" he cried. But, realizing that this would not help matters, he stopped short in the middle of a sentence and merely sighed. "Well — can sowing begin?" he asked after a pause.
"Behind Turkin tomorrow or the day after they might begin."
"And the clover?"
"I've sent Vassily and Mishka — they're sowing. Only I don't know if they'll get through it; it's so slushy."
"How many acres?"
"About fifteen."
"Why not sow all of it?" Levin cried.

That they were only sowing clover on fifteen acres, not on all forty-five, was even more annoying to him. Clover, as he knew both from books and from his own experience, never did well unless it was sown as early as possible, almost in the snow. And yet Levin could never get this done.
"There's no one to send. What can one do with such a set of peasants? Three haven't turned up. And then there's Semyon..."
"Well, you should have taken some men off the thatching."
"That's what I have done."
"Where are the peasants, then?"
"Five are making compôte" (which meant compost), "four are shifting the oats for fear of a touch of mildew, Konstantin Dmitrievitch."
Levin knew very well that "a touch of mildew" meant his English seed oats were already ruined. Again they had not done as he had ordered.
"But I told you during Lent to put in pipes," he cried.
"Don't put yourself out — we'll get it all done in time."

Levin waved a hand angrily, went into the granary to glance at the oats, and then to the stable. The oats were not yet spoiled. But the peasants were carrying the oats with spades when they could have just let them slide down into the lower granary; and after arranging for this to be done, and taking two workmen from there for sowing clover, Levin got over his vexation with the bailiff. Indeed, it was such a lovely day that one could not be angry.
"Ignat!" he called to the coachman, who, with his sleeves rolled up, was washing the carriage wheels. "Saddle me..."
"Which one, sir?"
"Well, let it be Kolpik."
"Yes, sir."

While they were saddling his horse, Levin again called up the bailiff, who was hanging about in sight, to make peace with him, and began talking to him about the spring operations ahead and his plans for the farm.

The wagons were to begin carting manure earlier, so as to get it all done before the early mowing. And the ploughing of the further land was to go on without a break so as to let it ripen lying fallow. And the mowing was to be all done by hired labor, not on half-profits. The bailiff listened attentively, and obviously made an effort to approve his employer's projects. But he still had that look Levin knew so well, that always irritated him — a look of hopelessness and despondency. That look said: "That's all very well, but as God wills."

Nothing mortified Levin so much as that tone. But it was the tone common to all the bailiffs he had ever had. They had all taken up that attitude to his plans, so by now he was not angered by it, but mortified, and felt all the more roused to struggle against this seemingly elemental force continually ranged against him, for which he could find no other expression than "as God wills."
"If we can manage it, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the bailiff said.
"Why ever shouldn't you manage it?"
"We positively must have another fifteen laborers. And they don't turn up. There were some here today asking seventy roubles for the summer."

Levin was silent. Again he was face to face with that opposing force. He knew that however much they tried, they could not hire more than forty — perhaps thirty-seven or thirty-eight — laborers for a reasonable price. About forty had already been taken on, and there were no more. But still he could not help fighting against it.
"Send to Sury, to Tchefirovka; if they don't come we'll have to look for them."
"Oh, I'll send, to be sure," Vassily Fedorovitch said despondently. "But there are the horses too — they're not good for much."

"We'll get some more. I know, of course," Levin added, laughing, "you always want to make do with as little and as poor as possible; but this year I'm not going to let you have your way. I'll see to everything myself."
"Why, I don't think you take much rest as it is. It cheers us up to work under the master's eye..."
"So they're sowing clover behind the Birch Dale? I'll go and have a look at them," he said, getting on to the little bay cob, Kolpik, who was led up by the coachman.
"You can't get across the streams, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the coachman shouted.
"All right, I'll go by the forest."

And Levin rode through the slush of the farmyard out the gate and into the open country, his good little horse, after his long inactivity, stepping out gallantly, snorting over the pools, and asking, as it were, for guidance. If Levin had felt happy before in the cattle pens and farmyard, he felt happier still in the open country. Swaying rhythmically with the ambling paces of his good little cob, drinking in the warm yet fresh scent of the snow and the air, as he rode through his forest over the crumbling, wasted snow still left in patches, covered with dissolving tracks, he rejoiced over every tree, with the moss reviving on its bark and the buds swelling on its shoots. When he came out of the forest, in the immense plain before him his grass fields stretched in an unbroken carpet of green, without one bare place or swamp, only spotted here and there in the hollows with patches of melting snow. He was not put out of temper even by the sight of peasants' horses and colts trampling down his young grass (he told a peasant he met to drive them out), nor by the sarcastic and stupid reply of the peasant Ipat, whom he met on the way, and asked, "Well, Ipat, shall we soon be sowing?" "We must get the ploughing done first, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," Ipat answered. The further he rode, the happier he became, and plans for the land rose to his mind, each better than the last: to plant all his fields with hedges along the southern borders so the snow would not lie under them; to divide them up into six fields of arable and three of pasture and hay; to build a cattle yard at the further end of the estate, and to dig a pond, and to construct movable pens for the cattle as a means of manuring the land. And then eight hundred acres of wheat, three hundred of potatoes, and four hundred of clover, and not one acre exhausted.

Absorbed in such dreams, carefully keeping his horse by the hedges so as not to trample his young crops, he rode up to the laborers who had been sent to sow clover. A cart with the seed in it was standing, not at the edge, but in the middle of the crop, and the winter corn had been torn up by the wheels and trampled by the horse. Both laborers were sitting in the hedge, probably smoking a pipe together. The earth in the cart, with which the seed was mixed, was not crushed to powder, but crusted together or stuck in clods. Seeing the master, the laborer Vassily went toward the cart, while Mishka set to work sowing. This was not as it should be, but with the laborers Levin seldom lost his temper. When Vassily came up, Levin told him to lead the horse to the hedge.
"It's all right, sir, it'll spring up again," Vassily replied.
"Please don't argue," Levin said, "just do as you're told."

"Yes, sir," Vassily answered, and he took the horse's head. "What a sowing, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," he said, hesitating; "first rate. Only it's a work to get about. You drag a ton of earth on your shoes."
"Why is it your earth isn't sifted?" Levin asked.
"Well, we crumble it up," Vassily answered, taking up some seed and rolling the earth in his palms.
Vassily was not to blame for their having filled his cart with unsifted earth, but still it was annoying.

Levin had more than once before tried a way he knew for stifling his anger and turning all that seemed dark right again, and he tried that way now. He watched how Mishka strode along, swinging the huge clods of earth that clung to each foot; and getting off his horse, he took the sieve from Vassily and started sowing himself.
"Where did you stop?"

Vassily pointed out the mark with his foot, and Levin set off as best he could, scattering seed across the land. Walking was as hard as on a bog, and by the time Levin had finished the row he was in a great heat, and he stopped and handed the sieve back to Vassily.
"Well, master, when summer's here, mind you don't scold me for these rows," said Vassily.
"Eh?" Levin said cheerily, already feeling the effect of his method.

"Why, you'll see come summertime. It'll look different. Look where I sowed last spring. How I did work at it! I do my best, Konstantin Dmitrievitch, you see, as I would for my own father. I don't like bad work myself, and I wouldn't let another man do it. What's good for the master's good for us too. To look out yonder now," Vassily said, pointing, "it does one's heart good."
"It's a lovely spring, Vassily."
"Why, it's a spring like the old men don't remember. I was up home; an old man up there has sown wheat too, about an acre of it. He said you wouldn't know it from rye."
"Have you been sowing wheat long?"
"Why, sir, you taught us the year before last. You gave me two measures. We sold about eight bushels and sowed a rood."
"Well, mind you crumble up the clods," Levin said, going toward his horse, "and keep an eye on Mishka. And if there's a good crop you shall have half a rouble for every acre."
"Humbly thankful. We are very well content, sir, as it is."
Levin got on his horse and rode toward the field with last year's clover, and the one ploughed ready for the spring corn.

The crop of clover coming up in the stubble was magnificent. It had survived everything, and stood up vividly green through the broken stalks of last year's wheat. The horse sank in up to the pasterns, and drew each hoof with a sucking sound out of the half-thawed ground. Over the ploughland riding was utterly impossible; the horse could only keep his footing where there was ice, and in the thawing furrows sank in deep at each step. The ploughland was in splendid condition; in a couple of days it would be fit for harrowing and sowing. Everything was capital, everything was cheering. Levin rode back across the streams, hoping the water would have gone down. And he did in fact get across, and startled two ducks. "There must be snipe too," he thought, and just as he reached the turning homeward he met the forest keeper, who confirmed his theory about the snipe.
Levin went home at a trot, so as to have time to eat his dinner and get his gun ready for the evening.
